growth_story.headline: Ireland's income per person rode foreign investment, crashed with its banks in 2008, then soared as multinationals booked more of their output there.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Ireland's income per person has grown in three eras: 5.5 percent a year over 1990–2005, -0.6 over 2006–2013 and 6.9 over 2014–2025. The IMF ties the first era to large inflows of foreign investment, low corporate tax rates, wage pacts and more people at work; after euro entry, growth came more from cheap credit and rising property prices. That boom ended in a banking crisis: income per person fell 6.4 percent in 2008 and 6.1 in 2009, and Ireland entered an IMF-supported programme in 2010. The third era began with a recovery, but its size owes much to multinational firms: the 23.5 percent jump in 2015 came mostly from companies moving assets to Ireland, which the IMF says did little for the underlying economy. Since then the figures have swung widely, from 14.6 percent in 2021 to -4.3 in 2023 and 10.5 in 2025, which the IMF ties to strong exports by multinational firms, leaving income per person at its highest level so far. Over the last decade growth averaged 5.1 percent a year, up from 2.7 in the decade before.

threads.title: Foreign investment and the Celtic Tiger
threads.text: In the 1990s Ireland drew in large flows of foreign investment, helped by low corporate tax rates and wage pacts, while unemployment fell and more people moved into work. Income per person grew 9.9 percent in 1997 and 9.3 in 1999.

threads.title: Credit boom and banking bust
threads.text: After euro entry, interest rates fell and growth leaned on borrowing and rising property prices, with banks funding the credit boom by borrowing heavily on international markets. When the property bubble burst the banks ran into trouble, the economy shrank and Ireland turned to an IMF-supported programme in 2010.

citations.title: Ireland: Ex Post Evaluation of Exceptional Access Under the 2010 Extended Arrangement; IMF Country Report No. 15/20
citations.quote: This was supported by a large credit expansion and a property price driven wealth effect.

citations.title: Ireland: Ex Post Evaluation of Exceptional Access Under the 2010 Extended Arrangement; IMF Country Report No. 15/20
citations.quote: Banking sector difficulties and the bursting of the real estate bubble took their toll on the broader economy.

threads.title: Multinationals move their assets in
threads.text: In 2015 large multinational firms moved intellectual property, such as patents, to Ireland, partly in response to global moves against tax avoidance. Measured income per person jumped 23.5 percent that year, but the IMF judged it a one-off shift with little effect on the underlying economy.

threads.title: Reliance on a few multinationals
threads.text: A few sectors led by foreign multinational firms produce much of Ireland's output, which puts growth and tax revenue at risk, so the headline figures swing with these firms' choices. Spending by people and firms at home has moved more steadily than the export side.

threads.title: Housing behind a growing population
threads.text: Ireland's population has grown fast and home building has not kept pace. The OECD says high housing costs could make the country less attractive to foreign firms and skilled workers.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 10.5 percent in 2025, after 1.0 in 2024. The IMF says strong exports by multinational firms drove the jump, as firms brought shipments forward, and that output then fell sharply in early 2026 as those exports returned to normal.

citations.title: Ireland: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; and Staff Report; IMF Country Report No. 26/156
citations.quote: Real GDP rose by 12.3 percent in 2025, largely driven by MNEs’ strong exports

citations.title: Ireland: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; and Staff Report; IMF Country Report No. 26/156
citations.quote: contracted by 17 percent (y-o-y) in 2026 Q1, reflecting a return to more normal levels of MNEs’ exports following front-loading last year

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person growing 6.9 percent a year over 2014–2025, and 5.1 over 2016–2025, the fastest of 11 structural peers. The sources say much of the output counted in Ireland belongs to the global operations of multinational firms. The IMF calls the 23.5 percent jump in 2015 a one-off shift with limited impact on the underlying economy, and it measures the home economy with separate gauges that rose much less than the data's 10.5 percent in 2025.
